crime.value: Death of an outsider on Bald Knob — apparently accidental (crushed by a lightning-split oak) but framed as a supernatural/ritual killing and secret burial; earlier a film director vanished the same way. Question: was this accident, ghost, or murder by the Andersons?
crime.quote: The big oak tree which lay on top of him had been split by a lightning bolt. Under it, Ed was crushed like a bug

victim.value: Ed, an arrogant Hollywood location scout who intended to bring a film crew and 'spoil' the hills — an outsider with contempt for locals, hence 'killable' by hill custom
victim.quote: "In this Godforsaken place," he said to himself, "the hillbillies will be glad for the chance at a little cash."

closed_world.value: An isolated Ozark hill farm and the taboo Bald Knob above it, near Ozark, Missouri (pop. 800), where outsiders are unwelcome and locals keep their own law
closed_world.quote: primitive passions and strong hatreds are bred in the hills, and old ideas and old grudges die hard

culprit_and_motive.value: Per the Andersons, the ghost of their hanged Bald Knobber son lured Ed under the oak; effectively Luke and the woman, who deliberately sent him up the hill to protect the hills from outsiders (as with the earlier movie director)
culprit_and_motive.quote: "It was our son again," the woman said with pride. "He lured that man under the oak tree."

resolution.value: No investigation or justice: the couple bury the body in the hill, evidence washed away by the storm, the folk-ritual chant closing the story
resolution.quote: "Get him out from there, Luke. We'll plant him in the hill, where we planted the other man."

investigator.value: No detective; an omniscient narrator with Ed the doomed outsider as viewpoint — reader learns the truth from the killers themselves
investigator.quote: Any of these local experts could have warned Ed about the risks he was taking, but he might not have listened

suspect_architecture.value: Effectively two living suspects plus a supernatural third: Luke Anderson and his wife ('Ma'), the elderly hill couple with motive (protecting the hills from outsiders and grief over their hanged son) and opportunity; the credited 'killer' is their dead son's ghost/Bald Knobber spirit. A prior victim (the earlier movie director) establishes pattern.
suspect_architecture.quote: "It was our son again," the woman said with pride. "He lured that man under the oak tree."

red_herring.value: The lightning-split oak presents the death as pure natural accident — reinforced by the storm, the 'rain crow' omen, and the washed-away footprints — misdirecting from the couple's complicity and the pattern of disappeared outsiders.
red_herring.quote: The big oak tree which lay on top of him had been split by a lightning bolt.

clue_fairness.value: Fairly seeded: the earlier movie's vanished director, the couple's veiled warnings, the son hanged as a Bald Knobber, the 'spirits never left' legend, and Luke's rain prediction are all given to the reader before the ending.
clue_fairness.quote: the director actually dropping out of sight, never to be seen again

social_world.value: Ozark hill country insularity versus Hollywood money: vigilante Bald Knobber self-policing replacing absent law, communal loyalty that refused to hang its own, and deep hostility to outsiders who 'spoil' the land.
social_world.quote: The hills don't tolerate no alien ways.

alibi.value: The couple's implicit alibi is that they stayed at the farmhouse and went to bed during the storm while Ed climbed alone — attributing the death to weather and to their son's spirit.
alibi.quote: Luke and the woman looked at one another wordlessly, and went to bed.

reveal_mechanic.value: Confession by casual dialogue at the corpse: the woman's proud statement plus 'where we planted the other man' retroactively converts an accident into serial disposal, sealed by the corn-planting chant.
reveal_mechanic.quote: "We'll plant him in the hill, where we planted the other man."

media_and_audience.value: Local folklore (the Bald Knobber legend, cursed hill, spirits) functions as the community's narrative cover; the earlier disaster was packaged by the press as sensational mystery that ironically saved the film at the box office.
media_and_audience.quote: That had caused quite a stir in the press. It was, in fact, the only thing which saved the movie from being a box-office disaster.

victims_enemies.value: Ed, a Hollywood location scout, is an outsider whose contempt for the hill people and plan to 'spoil' the land makes enemies of the entire community — chiefly Luke and his wife, who lost their son to outsider-brought law and grief, and who already disposed of a previous movie man the same way.
victims_enemies.quote: "Just like he done before, with that other movie man."

suspect_wounds.value: Luke and Ma carry the wound of a hanged son and a desecrated Bald Knob; their courtesy masks the grievance the visitor's arrival reactivates.
suspect_wounds.quote: "The Bald Knobbers came to trial, and the jury said they had to be hanged. One of those was our son."

unreliable_frame.value: The wife's folklore narration is the frame: she tells the Bald Knobber legend as history and warning while concealing that she and Luke are steering Ed to his death; her 'it was our son again' attributes to a ghost what her own manipulation accomplished.
unreliable_frame.quote: "Go, if you want." There was warning in her tone—and promise.

setting_as_constraint.value: Remote Ozark hill country: no witnesses, no law nearby, a bald knob shunned by locals, and a spring thunderstorm that erases footprints — the couple exploit local knowledge and terrain to make murder indistinguishable from accident.
setting_as_constraint.quote: Ed's footprints were washed away. There was no sign that anyone had been there before them.

evidence_type.value: Environmental/physical: the lightning-split oak crushing the body reads as natural accident; the only real evidence is the couple's own admission and the burial site of the earlier victim.
evidence_type.quote: The big oak tree which lay on top of him had been split by a lightning bolt.

false_suspect.value: The vanished son / the Bald Knobber ghost is offered as the 'culprit', deflecting from the living couple who engineered the death.
false_suspect.quote: "It was our son again," the woman said with pride. "He lured that man under the oak tree."

technical_detail.value: Hill-country weather lore: the rain crow foretells a storm, and any hill man knows not to shelter under a tree in a thunderstorm — the ignorance of this makes the method work.
technical_detail.quote: "Any hill man knows better than to go under a tree in a thunderstorm."

moral_ambiguity.value: The couple kill to protect land, livelihood and a way of life from developers who 'spoil' the hills, and out of unhealed grief for a son hanged by outsiders' law — defense of home rather than malice.
moral_ambiguity.quote: "Spoilt for living. Spoilt for farming. Spoilt for looking at. You think to do that here...?"
